title: Vicky Kaushal Has Vanished Into the Wilderness. He'll Return as a God.
excerpt: The actor just locked 18 months of his life — six months of physical transformation, twelve months of shooting — to play the immortal warrior-sage Parashurama in Maddock Films' most ambitious project ever. Shraddha Kapoor may be joining him. Here's everything we know.
body:
There is a version of Vicky Kaushal that Bollywood has gotten very comfortable with. The brooding officer. The charming husband. The man who can cry on cue and make you believe every tear. That version of Vicky is about to be incinerated.

Starting this month, Kaushal has entered what might be the most extreme commitment any Hindi film actor has made in years: an eighteen-month lockout — no other films, no brand shoots, no distractions — dedicated entirely to Mahavatar, the mythological epic in which he will play Chiranjeevi Parashurama, the sixth avatar of Vishnu and one of Hinduism's seven immortals.

The first six months are preparation. Physical transformation. Weapons training. Workshops with director Amar Kaushik, who has spent the better part of a year on pre-production — designing sets, forging (literally) the weapons Parashurama will carry, mapping out a world that blends ancient scripture with blockbuster spectacle. "The prep is going on for six to seven months," Kaushik has said. "We have worked on the set design, weapon design, how every character would look. The scripting is done. Yet, we need more time."

When cameras finally roll in January 2027, Kaushal intends to stay inside the character until December. No side projects. No cameos. Total immersion. It's the kind of commitment you associate with Daniel Day-Lewis disappearing into Lincoln or Christian Bale rebuilding his body for every role — except here, the scale isn't a prestige Oscar drama. It's a full-blown Indian mythological war epic produced by Maddock Films and backed by the man who built the Stree universe, Dinesh Vijan.

From Bhansali's Set to the Forge

The timing is everything. Kaushal is expected to wrap Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Love and War — itself a mammoth production with a reported budget north of ₹425 crore, co-starring Ranbir Kapoor and Alia Bhatt — just in time to pivot into Mahavatar prep. He walks off one of Bollywood's most lavish sets and directly into a forge.

That transition tells you something about where Vicky's head is. He's not interested in volume anymore. He's not chasing three releases a year. He's betting his entire 2026 and 2027 on two films that demand everything — body, voice, emotional range, physical endurance. Both are period pieces. Both require transformation. And both are directed by filmmakers who don't settle.

The Character: Parashurama

For the uninitiated — and this matters for any NRI who grew up with Amar Chitra Katha but hasn't revisited the Dashavatara since — Parashurama is not your standard mythological hero. He's Vishnu's angriest incarnation. A Brahmin warrior who picked up an axe (the parshu, a divine gift) and waged war against the Kshatriya kings who had become corrupt and oppressive. He is rage fused with righteousness, asceticism married to violence.

He is also one of the Chiranjivi — the immortals who are said to still walk the earth, waiting to appear at the end of the Kali Yuga as the guru of Vishnu's final avatar, Kalki. If you watched Kalki 2898 AD, you already know this mythology has box office legs. Nag Ashwin understood it. Now Kaushik and Vijan are going deeper.

This isn't a retelling. It's a reclamation. And Kaushal — lean, intense, capable of projecting both stillness and fury — is the right vessel for it.

Shraddha Kapoor in the Frame

According to multiple reports, Shraddha Kapoor is in advanced talks to play the female lead opposite Kaushal. If she signs on, it would mark their first on-screen pairing — and given that both actors sit comfortably in the ₹200-crore-plus club, the commercial math is staggering. Shraddha, coming off the cultural phenomenon of Stree 2 (also an Amar Kaushik film, also Maddock), already has a working relationship with this team. The fit is almost too clean.

A Bigger Shift

Vicky isn't alone in this kind of bet. Ranveer Singh has simultaneously committed to Pralay, a ₹300-crore post-apocalyptic thriller that begins filming in August. Bollywood's leading men are moving away from the three-films-a-year assembly line and toward singular, high-stakes, career-defining swings. It's the Hollywood model — one film, one year, one shot at something that matters.

For the diaspora, this shift is significant. These aren't films you'll catch on OTT three months later and forget. Mahavatar, if it lands, will be a theatrical event — the kind of mythological spectacle that demands a big screen, a packed house, and the collective gasp of an audience watching something they haven't seen before.

Mahavatar is expected to arrive in 2027 — possibly Independence Day weekend, which would put it in direct competition with Maddock's own Stree 3. That scheduling headache is a problem for later. Right now, somewhere in Mumbai, Vicky Kaushal is tearing himself apart and putting something new together.

When he re-emerges, he won't be the charming leading man anymore. He'll be carrying an axe.
